episodes.request: Someone on the data team asked what the period 2026-W01 stands for in dateseq; they expected it to be the first seven days of January. Can you check how dateseq reads it? Please don't change anything.

steps.thought: The README describes the period syntax.
steps.output:
# dateseq

Prints the dates of a period, one per line, for backfills, report jobs, and shell
loops:

    for day in $(python3 -m dateseq list 2026-03); do
        ./load_day.sh "$day"
    done

## Usage

    python3 -m dateseq list 2026-03-02 2026-03-06     # five dates, both ends included
    python3 -m dateseq list 2026-03                   # every date of March 2026
    python3 -m dateseq list 2026-W10                  # Monday to Sunday of ISO week 10
    python3 -m dateseq list 2026-03 2026-05           # 1 March to 31 May
    python3 -m dateseq list 2026-03 --weekdays        # Monday to Friday only
    python3 -m dateseq list 2026-W10 --format compact # 20260302, 20260303, ...
    python3 -m dateseq count 2026-03 --weekdays       # how many weekdays March has

START and END are each a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a month (`YYYY-MM`), or an ISO week
(`YYYY-Www`). A range runs from the first date of START to the last date of END, and
both ends are included. Without END it covers the period START alone. A range whose
end comes before its start has no dates.

`--format` is one of:

| name | example |
| --- | --- |
| `iso` (default) | `2026-03-02` |
| `compact` | `20260302` |
| `eu` | `02.03.2026` |
| `weekday` | `Mon 2026-03-02` |

A date or period that cannot be read stops the command with a message, and the
command exits with status 2.

## Library

    from datetime import date
    from dateseq.ranges import date_range, day_count, weekdays

    list(date_range(date(2026, 3, 2), date(2026, 3, 6)))   # 2 March to 6 March
    day_count(date(2026, 3, 1), date(2026, 3, 31))         # 31

`dateseq.periods.parse_period("2026-W10")` returns the first and the last date of a
period.

## Development

    python3 -m pytest -v

The package lives in `src/dateseq/` and uses only the standard library.

finish.thought: The week is an ISO week, which explains the surprise.
finish.report: 2026-W01 is an ISO week, not the first days of January. parse_period in src/dateseq/periods.py matches YYYY-Www with _WEEK and hands it to _week, which takes the Monday from date.fromisocalendar(2026, 1, 1) and adds six days. ISO week 1 is the week that contains the year's first Thursday, and 1 January 2026 is a Thursday, so 2026-W01 runs from Monday 29 December 2025 to Sunday 4 January 2026. If they mean calendar dates, they should give dates (YYYY-MM-DD) instead of a week. _week also checks the number against weeks_in: 2026 is a long year with weeks 01 to 53, while 2027-W53 is rejected with an error.

episodes.request: Which output formats does dateseq support? Finance would like US-style dates such as 03/02/2026. Where would that go?

finish.thought: Adding a format is one function and one table entry.
finish.report: There are four formats: iso (the default, 2026-03-02), compact (20260302), eu (02.03.2026), and weekday (Mon 2026-03-02). They are the FORMATS table in src/dateseq/formats.py. A US style would be one more function there, for example us(day) returning f"{day.month:02d}/{day.day:02d}/{day.year:04d}", plus an entry "us": us in FORMATS. The command line needs no change: build_parser in src/dateseq/cli.py takes the choices of --format from sorted(FORMATS), and main passes args.format to format_dates. The format table in the README lists every format, so it should get a row for the new one.

finish.report: Those three modules have 27 test functions: 11 in tests/test_cli.py, 4 in tests/test_formats.py, and 12 in tests/test_periods.py. Two are parametrized: test_each_format in tests/test_formats.py runs once per format (4 cases) and test_parse_date_rejects_other_forms in tests/test_periods.py runs once per rejected form (6 cases), so pytest runs 35 tests from these modules. The command-line tests call main directly and read the output with capsys, so they need no temporary files.
